newsitem.title: CANADA: Nortel's incoming CEO has big shoes to fill.
newsitem.headline: Nortel's incoming CEO has big shoes to fill.

text.p: Soft-spoken John Roth has big shoes to fill when he becomes Northern Telecom Ltd. chief executive, replacing Jean Monty, who is credited with turning around the Canadian telecommunications equipment company.

Monty, 49, took the helm of a troubled firm overly dependent on a slowing core business -- central office switching -- and re-shaped it into a nimble and high-growth contender in the fast-changing telecom equipment world.

In the second quarter of 1993, soon after Monty replaced Paul Stern, the company took $940 million in charges to cover a major software revamp and a goodwill writedown on its 1991 acquisition of STC Plc.

Stern was criticised for the huge charge and the company's late entry into the wireless and broadband (multimedia) markets. But Nortel is back to record profitability and analysts are keen to know if Roth can chart the same successful course as Monty.

The Alberta-born Roth, 54, will be the first Nortel chief executive in more than 20 years to have risen through the ranks. The 28-year company veteran shook up Nortel's wireless division after it missed out on the early growth of the analogue (early cellular phone) market.
"I think continuity shouldn't be a problem," Roth, who was tapped by Monty for the top job two years ago and given board approval last year, said in a recent interview.
Roth, who has became Nortel president in March, becomes chief executive in October.
Monty, who was parachuted in from Bell Canada, the telephone company arm of Nortel's parent BCE Inc., is returning to the BCE group in a so far unspecified capacity.
Roth said that while Monty, who was popular with the financial community, was more of a "financial engineer" charged with cleaning up Nortel's balance sheet, his focus has been on products.
After a stint at RCA's antenna division where he designed the optics for satellite-borne antennas, Roth joined the research and development facility at then-Northern Electric.
Roth since 1994 has effectively run 66 percent of the company in terms of revenues. South America and Europe have since been folded into his areas of responsibility.
Roth's two-pronged approach to the future places an even greater emphasis on the issues Monty brought to the fore at Nortel -- customer service and a complete product portfolio.
"My goal when my time comes to lead Nortel is I want to make sure that Nortel is well-positioned with a portfolio that will be appropriate going into the next century," Roth said.

"Fields like wireless are going to dominate. The Internet is going to dominate communications. The international networks are going to dominate telecommunications. Those are the areas that Northern has to be well-positioned in."
